examples.input_text:
Universal Declaration of Human Rights
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) is a milestone document in the history of human rights. Drafted by representatives with different legal and cultural backgrounds from all regions of the world, the Declaration was proclaimed by the United Nations General Assembly in Paris on 10 December 1948 (General Assembly resolution 217 A) as a common standard of achievements for all peoples and all nations. It sets out, for the first time, fundamental human rights to be universally protected and it has been translated into over 500 languages. The UDHR is widely recognized as having inspired, and paved the way for, the adoption of more than seventy human rights treaties, applied today on a permanent basis at global and regional levels (all containing references to it in their preambles). 

Preamble
Whereas recognition of the inherent dignity and of the equal and inalienable rights of all members of the human family is the foundation of freedom, justice and peace in the world,

Whereas disregard and contempt for human rights have resulted in barbarous acts which have outraged the conscience of mankind, and the advent of a world in which human beings shall enjoy freedom of speech and belief and freedom from fear and want has been proclaimed as the highest aspiration of the common people,

Whereas it is essential, if man is not to be compelled to have recourse, as a last resort, to rebellion against tyranny and oppression, that human rights should be protected by the rule of law,

Whereas it is essential to promote the development of friendly relations between nations,

Whereas the peoples of the United Nations have in the Charter reaffirmed their faith in fundamental human rights, in the dignity and worth of the human person and in the equal rights of men and women and have determined to promote social progress and better standards of life in larger freedom,

Whereas Member States have pledged themselves to achieve, in co-operation with the United Nations, the promotion of universal respect for and observance of human rights and fundamental freedoms,

Whereas a common understanding of these rights and freedoms is of the greatest importance for the full realization of this pledge,

Now, therefore,

The General Assembly,

Proclaims this Universal Declaration of Human Rights as a common standard of achievement for all peoples and all nations, to the end that every individual and every organ of society, keeping this Declaration constantly in mind, shall strive by teaching and education to promote respect for these rights and freedoms and by progressive measures, national and international, to secure their universal and effective recognition and observance, both among the peoples of Member States themselves and among the peoples of territories under their jurisdiction. 

Article 1
All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights. They are endowed with reason and conscience and should act towards one another in a spirit of brotherhood.

Article 2
Everyone is entitled to all the rights and freedoms set forth in this Declaration, without distinction of any kind, such as race, colour, sex, language, religion, political or other opinion, national or social origin, property, birth or other status. Furthermore, no distinction shall be made on the basis of the political, jurisdictional or international status of the country or territory to which a person belongs, whether it be independent, trust, non-self-governing or under any other limitation of sovereignty.

Article 3
Everyone has the right to life, liberty and security of person.

Article 4
No one shall be held in slavery or servitude; slavery and the slave trade shall be prohibited in all their forms.

Article 5
No one shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.

Article 6
Everyone has the right to recognition everywhere as a person before the law.

Article 7
All are equal before the law and are entitled without any discrimination to equal protection of the law. All are entitled to equal protection against any discrimination in violation of this Declaration and against any incitement to such discrimination.

Article 8
Everyone has the right to an effective remedy by the competent national tribunals for acts violating the fundamental rights granted him by the constitution or by law.

Article 9
No one shall be subjected to arbitrary arrest, detention or exile.

Article 10
Everyone is entitled in full equality to a fair and public hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal, in the determination of his rights and obligations and of any criminal charge against him.

Article 11
Everyone charged with a penal offence has the right to be presumed innocent until proved guilty according to law in a public trial at which he has had all the guarantees necessary for his defence.
No one shall be held guilty of any penal offence on account of any act or omission which did not constitute a penal offence, under national or international law, at the time when it was committed. Nor shall a heavier penalty be imposed than the one that was applicable at the time the penal offence was committed.
Article 12
No one shall be subjected to arbitrary interference with his privacy, family, home or correspondence, nor to attacks upon his honour and reputation. Everyone has the right to the protection of the law against such interference or attacks.

Article 13
Everyone has the right to freedom of movement and residence within the borders of each state.
Everyone has the right to leave any country, including his own, and to return to his country.
Article 14
Everyone has the right to seek and to enjoy in other countries asylum from persecution.
This right may not be invoked in the case of prosecutions genuinely arising from non-political crimes or from acts contrary to the purposes and principles of the United Nations.
Article 15
Everyone has the right to a nationality.
No one shall be arbitrarily deprived of his nationality nor denied the right to change his nationality.
Article 16
Men and women of full age, without any limitation due to race, nationality or religion, have the right to marry and to found a family. They are entitled to equal rights as to marriage, during marriage and at its dissolution.
Marriage shall be entered into only with the free and full consent of the intending spouses.
The family is the natural and fundamental group unit of society and is entitled to protection by society and the State.
Article 17
Everyone has the right to own property alone as well as in association with others.
No one shall be arbitrarily deprived of his property.
Article 18
Everyone has the right to freedom of thought, conscience and religion; this right includes freedom to change his religion or belief, and freedom, either alone or in community with others and in public or private, to manifest his religion or belief in teaching, practice, worship and observance.

Article 19
Everyone has the right to freedom of opinion and expression; this right includes freedom to hold opinions without interference and to seek, receive and impart information and ideas through any media and regardless of frontiers.

Article 20
Everyone has the right to freedom of peaceful assembly and association.
No one may be compelled to belong to an association.
Article 21
Everyone has the right to take part in the government of his country, directly or through freely chosen representatives.
Everyone has the right of equal access to public service in his country.
The will of the people shall be the basis of the authority of government; this will shall be expressed in periodic and genuine elections which shall be by universal and equal suffrage and shall be held by secret vote or by equivalent free voting procedures.
Article 22
Everyone, as a member of society, has the right to social security and is entitled to realization, through national effort and international co-operation and in accordance with the organization and resources of each State, of the economic, social and cultural rights indispensable for his dignity and the free development of his personality.

Article 23
Everyone has the right to work, to free choice of employment, to just and favourable conditions of work and to protection against unemployment.
Everyone, without any discrimination, has the right to equal pay for equal work.
Everyone who works has the right to just and favourable remuneration ensuring for himself and his family an existence worthy of human dignity, and supplemented, if necessary, by other means of social protection.
Everyone has the right to form and to join trade unions for the protection of his interests.
Article 24
Everyone has the right to rest and leisure, including reasonable limitation of working hours and periodic holidays with pay.

Article 25
Everyone has the right to a standard of living adequate for the health and well-being of himself and of his family, including food, clothing, housing and medical care and necessary social services, and the right to security in the event of unemployment, sickness, disability, widowhood, old age or other lack of livelihood in circumstances beyond his control.
Motherhood and childhood are entitled to special care and assistance. All children, whether born in or out of wedlock, shall enjoy the same social protection.
Article 26
Everyone has the right to education. Education shall be free, at least in the elementary and fundamental stages. Elementary education shall be compulsory. Technical and professional education shall be made generally available and higher education shall be equally accessible to all on the basis of merit.
Education shall be directed to the full development of the human personality and to the strengthening of respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms. It shall promote understanding, tolerance and friendship among all nations, racial or religious groups, and shall further the activities of the United Nations for the maintenance of peace.
Parents have a prior right to choose the kind of education that shall be given to their children.
Article 27
Everyone has the right freely to participate in the cultural life of the community, to enjoy the arts and to share in scientific advancement and its benefits.
Everyone has the right to the protection of the moral and material interests resulting from any scientific, literary or artistic production of which he is the author.
Article 28
Everyone is entitled to a social and international order in which the rights and freedoms set forth in this Declaration can be fully realized.

Article 29
Everyone has duties to the community in which alone the free and full development of his personality is possible.
In the exercise of his rights and freedoms, everyone shall be subject only to such limitations as are determined by law solely for the purpose of securing due recognition and respect for the rights and freedoms of others and of meeting the just requirements of morality, public order and the general welfare in a democratic society.
These rights and freedoms may in no case be exercised contrary to the purposes and principles of the United Nations.
Article 30
Nothing in this Declaration may be interpreted as implying for any State, group or person any right to engage in any activity or to perform any act aimed at the destruction of any of the rights and freedoms set forth herein.

entities.description: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) is a milestone document in the history of human rights, proclaimed by the United Nations General Assembly in Paris on 10 December 1948 as General Assembly resolution 217 A. It sets out, for the first time, fundamental human rights to be universally protected, has been translated into over 500 languages, and is recognized as having inspired more than seventy human rights treaties. The text includes its preamble and Articles 1–30, which enumerate a wide range of civil, political, economic, social and cultural rights and corresponding limitations and duties.

"UDHR" is the acronym used in the text to refer to the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, the 1948 General Assembly declaration that sets out fundamental human rights and has inspired numerous human rights treaties.

The United Nations General Assembly is the main deliberative body of the United Nations that proclaimed the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in Paris on 10 December 1948, through General Assembly resolution 217 A. In the text it is referred to simply as "The General Assembly" when it proclaims the UDHR as a common standard of achievement and calls upon every individual and organ of society to promote respect for and observance of the rights and freedoms it contains.
Paris is the city named as the place where the United Nations General Assembly proclaimed the Universal Declaration of Human Rights on 10 December 1948.
10 December 1948 is the date on which the United Nations General Assembly proclaimed the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in Paris, adopting it as General Assembly resolution 217 A.
General Assembly resolution 217 A is the formal resolution number under which the United Nations General Assembly proclaimed the Universal Declaration of Human Rights on 10 December 1948.
"Over 500" refers to the approximate number of languages into which the Universal Declaration of Human Rights has been translated, indicating its wide dissemination.

"More than seventy" human rights treaties are said to have been adopted after and inspired by the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. These treaties operate at global and regional levels on a permanent basis and contain references to the UDHR in their preambles.

The United Nations is the international organization whose General Assembly adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. The text notes that the peoples of the United Nations reaffirmed in the Charter their faith in fundamental human rights, the dignity and worth of the human person, and the equal rights of men and women, and that Member States cooperate with the United Nations to promote universal respect for and observance of human rights and fundamental freedoms, including through education and other activities for the maintenance of peace.

The Charter of the United Nations is referenced as the document in which the peoples of the United Nations reaffirm their faith in fundamental human rights, the dignity and worth of the human person, and the equal rights of men and women, and determine to promote social progress and better standards of life in larger freedom.

entities.entity_name: Member States of the United Nations
entities.description: Member States of the United Nations are the States that belong to the United Nations. In the text they are described as having pledged themselves, in cooperation with the United Nations, to achieve the promotion of universal respect for and observance of human rights and fundamental freedoms, and as responsible for securing recognition and observance of the rights in the Declaration among their own peoples and those of territories under their jurisdiction.

The General Assembly, as mentioned in the proclamation section, refers to the United Nations General Assembly acting to proclaim the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as a common standard of achievement and calling upon every individual and organ of society to promote and secure recognition and observance of the rights and freedoms it sets forth.

Human rights are described as the equal and inalienable rights of all members of the human family, recognition of which forms the foundation of freedom, justice and peace in the world. The text stresses that disregard and contempt for human rights have resulted in barbarous acts, that they must be protected by the rule of law, and then enumerates specific civil, political, economic, social and cultural rights in the articles of the Declaration.

Freedom is presented as a foundational condition and value, associated with justice and peace and with larger freedom in social progress and standards of life. The preamble and articles refer to freedom of speech and belief, freedom from fear and want, freedom of movement, and various specific freedoms that together characterize the envisioned world order.

Justice is cited in the preamble as one of the foundations, along with freedom and peace, of the world order based on recognition of the inherent dignity and equal and inalienable rights of all members of the human family.

Peace is described as one of the foundations, along with freedom and justice, of the world order that follows from recognizing the inherent dignity and equal and inalienable rights of all members of the human family. The text also mentions the activities of the United Nations for the maintenance of peace, which education should further.

The rule of law is described as the framework of legal protection for human rights that is essential so that people are not compelled, as a last resort, to rebellion against tyranny and oppression. It refers broadly to governance by laws that safeguard rights rather than arbitrary power.

Tyranny is mentioned in the preamble as a condition of oppressive power that, together with oppression, could compel people to rebellion if human rights are not protected by the rule of law. The Declaration aims to prevent such conditions.
Oppression is mentioned alongside tyranny in the preamble as a condition that could lead people to rebellion if human rights are not protected by the rule of law.

The human family is a collective term for all members of humanity. The text states that recognition of the inherent dignity and of the equal and inalienable rights of all members of the human family is the foundation of freedom, justice and peace in the world.

Nations refers to countries or States considered as political communities. The text mentions friendly relations between nations, describes the Declaration as a common standard for all nations, and calls for education to promote understanding, tolerance and friendship among all nations.

Peoples refers to populations or communities of persons, including the peoples of the United Nations and the peoples within Member States and territories under their jurisdiction. The text describes the Declaration as a common standard of achievement for all peoples, refers to the peoples of the United Nations reaffirming their faith in fundamental human rights, and notes that the will of the people is the basis of the authority of government.

entities.entity_name: Territories under the jurisdiction of Member States
entities.description: Territories under the jurisdiction of Member States are geographical areas over which Member States exercise authority. The proclamation states that the rights and freedoms in the Declaration are to be secured both among the peoples of Member States and among the peoples of territories under their jurisdiction.

The preambles of human rights treaties are the introductory parts of more than seventy human rights treaties that, according to the text, all contain references to the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, demonstrating its influence on later instruments.

entities.entity_name: Article 1 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights
entities.description: Article 1 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights is the provision stating that all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights, are endowed with reason and conscience, and should act towards one another in a spirit of brotherhood.

entities.entity_name: Article 2 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights
entities.description: Article 2 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights provides that everyone is entitled to all the rights and freedoms set forth in the Declaration without distinction of any kind, such as race, colour, sex, language, religion, political or other opinion, national or social origin, property, birth or other status, and that no distinction shall be made on the basis of the political, jurisdictional or international status of the country or territory to which a person belongs.

entities.entity_name: Article 3 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights
entities.description: Article 3 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights states that everyone has the right to life, liberty and security of person.

entities.entity_name: Article 4 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights
entities.description: Article 4 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights provides that no one shall be held in slavery or servitude and that slavery and the slave trade shall be prohibited in all their forms.

entities.entity_name: Article 5 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights
entities.description: Article 5 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights declares that no one shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.

entities.entity_name: Article 6 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights
entities.description: Article 6 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights affirms that everyone has the right to recognition everywhere as a person before the law.

entities.entity_name: Article 7 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights
entities.description: Article 7 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights states that all are equal before the law and are entitled without any discrimination to equal protection of the law, including equal protection against discrimination in violation of the Declaration and against any incitement to such discrimination.

entities.entity_name: Article 8 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights
entities.description: Article 8 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights guarantees everyone the right to an effective remedy by competent national tribunals for acts violating fundamental rights granted by the constitution or by law.

entities.entity_name: Article 9 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights
entities.description: Article 9 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights states that no one shall be subjected to arbitrary arrest, detention or exile.

entities.entity_name: Article 10 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights
entities.description: Article 10 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights provides that everyone is entitled, in full equality, to a fair and public hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal in the determination of their rights and obligations and of any criminal charge against them.

entities.entity_name: Article 11 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights
entities.description: Article 11 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights sets out that everyone charged with a penal offence has the right to be presumed innocent until proved guilty according to law in a public trial with all guarantees necessary for their defence, and that no one shall be held guilty of a penal offence for acts or omissions that were not offences under national or international law at the time, nor be subjected to a heavier penalty than that applicable when the offence was committed.

entities.entity_name: Article 12 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights
entities.description: Article 12 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights prohibits arbitrary interference with a person's privacy, family, home or correspondence, as well as attacks upon their honour and reputation, and provides that everyone has the right to the protection of the law against such interference or attacks.

entities.entity_name: Article 13 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights
entities.description: Article 13 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights establishes that everyone has the right to freedom of movement and residence within the borders of each state and the right to leave any country, including their own, and to return to their country.

entities.entity_name: Article 14 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights
entities.description: Article 14 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights affirms that everyone has the right to seek and enjoy asylum in other countries from persecution, but specifies that this right may not be invoked for prosecutions genuinely arising from non-political crimes or acts contrary to the purposes and principles of the United Nations.

entities.entity_name: Article 15 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights
entities.description: Article 15 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights states that everyone has the right to a nationality and that no one shall be arbitrarily deprived of their nationality or denied the right to change it.

entities.entity_name: Article 16 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights
entities.description: Article 16 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights provides that men and women of full age, without limitation due to race, nationality or religion, have the right to marry and to found a family, are entitled to equal rights during marriage and at its dissolution, requires that marriage be entered into only with the free and full consent of the intending spouses, and declares the family to be the natural and fundamental group unit of society entitled to protection by society and the State.

entities.entity_name: Article 17 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights
entities.description: Article 17 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights states that everyone has the right to own property alone as well as in association with others and that no one shall be arbitrarily deprived of their property.

entities.entity_name: Article 18 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights
entities.description: Article 18 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights affirms the right to freedom of thought, conscience and religion, including freedom to change one’s religion or belief and to manifest religion or belief in teaching, practice, worship and observance, alone or with others, in public or private.

entities.entity_name: Article 19 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights
entities.description: Article 19 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights guarantees the right to freedom of opinion and expression, including the freedom to hold opinions without interference and to seek, receive and impart information and ideas through any media and regardless of frontiers.

entities.entity_name: Article 20 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights
entities.description: Article 20 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights provides that everyone has the right to freedom of peaceful assembly and association and that no one may be compelled to belong to an association.

entities.entity_name: Article 21 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights
entities.description: Article 21 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights sets out that everyone has the right to take part in the government of their country directly or through freely chosen representatives, the right of equal access to public service, and that the will of the people shall be the basis of the authority of government, expressed in periodic and genuine elections with universal and equal suffrage and secret or equivalent free voting procedures.

entities.entity_name: Article 22 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights
entities.description: Article 22 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights provides that everyone, as a member of society, has the right to social security and is entitled to realization, through national effort and international cooperation and in accordance with the organization and resources of each State, of the economic, social and cultural rights indispensable for their dignity and the free development of their personality.

entities.entity_name: Article 23 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights
entities.description: Article 23 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights states that everyone has the right to work, to free choice of employment, to just and favourable conditions of work and to protection against unemployment; to equal pay for equal work without discrimination; to just and favourable remuneration ensuring an existence worthy of human dignity for themselves and their family, supplemented if necessary by social protection; and to form and join trade unions for the protection of their interests.

entities.entity_name: Article 24 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights
entities.description: Article 24 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights affirms that everyone has the right to rest and leisure, including reasonable limitation of working hours and periodic holidays with pay.

entities.entity_name: Article 25 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights
entities.description: Article 25 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights states that everyone has the right to a standard of living adequate for the health and well-being of themselves and their family, including food, clothing, housing, medical care and necessary social services, and to security in the event of unemployment, sickness, disability, widowhood, old age or other lack of livelihood beyond their control. It also states that motherhood and childhood are entitled to special care and assistance and that all children, whether born in or out of wedlock, shall enjoy the same social protection.

entities.entity_name: Article 26 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights
entities.description: Article 26 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights provides that everyone has the right to education; that education shall be free, at least in the elementary and fundamental stages, with compulsory elementary education; that technical and professional education shall be generally available and higher education shall be equally accessible to all on the basis of merit; that education shall be directed to the full development of the human personality and the strengthening of respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms; that it shall promote understanding, tolerance and friendship among all nations and racial or religious groups and further the activities of the United Nations for the maintenance of peace; and that parents have a prior right to choose the kind of education given to their children.

entities.entity_name: Article 27 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights
entities.description: Article 27 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights states that everyone has the right freely to participate in the cultural life of the community, to enjoy the arts and to share in scientific advancement and its benefits, and that everyone has the right to the protection of the moral and material interests resulting from any scientific, literary or artistic production of which they are the author.

entities.entity_name: Article 28 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights
entities.description: Article 28 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights affirms that everyone is entitled to a social and international order in which the rights and freedoms set forth in the Declaration can be fully realized.

entities.entity_name: Article 29 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights
entities.description: Article 29 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights provides that everyone has duties to the community in which alone the free and full development of their personality is possible; that in exercising rights and freedoms, individuals shall be subject only to limitations determined by law for securing recognition and respect for the rights and freedoms of others and for meeting the just requirements of morality, public order and the general welfare in a democratic society; and that these rights and freedoms may in no case be exercised contrary to the purposes and principles of the United Nations.

entities.entity_name: Article 30 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights
entities.description: Article 30 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights states that nothing in the Declaration may be interpreted as implying for any State, group or person any right to engage in any activity or to perform any act aimed at the destruction of any of the rights and freedoms set forth in it.

Freedom of speech is mentioned in the preamble as part of the envisioned world in which human beings shall enjoy freedom of speech and belief and freedom from fear and want, described as the highest aspiration of the common people.

Freedom of belief is mentioned in the preamble, paired with freedom of speech and with freedom from fear and want, as part of the highest aspiration of the common people in a world where human beings enjoy these freedoms.

Freedom from fear is cited in the preamble as one of the conditions proclaimed as the highest aspiration of the common people, referring to a world in which human beings enjoy freedom of speech and belief and freedom from fear and want.

Freedom from want is cited in the preamble as part of the highest aspiration of the common people, referring to a world in which human beings enjoy freedom of speech and belief and freedom from fear and want.

Slavery is the condition prohibited in Article 4 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, which states that no one shall be held in slavery or servitude and that slavery and the slave trade shall be prohibited in all their forms.
The slave trade is the practice of trading in human beings as property, which Article 4 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights states shall be prohibited in all its forms along with slavery.

Torture is one of the acts prohibited in Article 5 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, which states that no one shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.

entities.entity_name: Cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment
entities.description: Cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment refers to forms of abuse or penalties that violate human dignity. Article 5 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights prohibits subjecting anyone to such treatment or punishment.
Arbitrary arrest is a prohibited practice under Article 9 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, which states that no one shall be subjected to arbitrary arrest, detention or exile.
Arbitrary detention is a prohibited practice under Article 9 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, which states that no one shall be subjected to arbitrary arrest, detention or exile.

Exile is listed in Article 9 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as a form of arbitrary action from which individuals must be protected, referring to being compelled to leave or remain outside one’s country.

A penal offence is a criminal offence under law. Article 11 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights states that everyone charged with a penal offence has the right to be presumed innocent until proved guilty and that no one shall be held guilty of any penal offence for acts or omissions that did not constitute a penal offence at the time, nor be subjected to a heavier penalty than was applicable then.

A heavier penalty refers to a more severe punishment than the one applicable at the time the penal offence was committed. Article 11 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights prohibits imposing such a heavier penalty.

Freedom of movement is the right, set out in Article 13 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, of everyone to move and reside within the borders of each state and to leave any country and return to their own.

Asylum from persecution is described in Article 14 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as the right to seek and enjoy asylum in other countries from persecution, subject to limits where prosecutions arise from non-political crimes or from acts contrary to the purposes and principles of the United Nations.

Nationality is described in Article 15 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as something everyone has a right to, including the right not to be arbitrarily deprived of nationality or denied the right to change it.

Marriage is mentioned in Article 16 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as a right of men and women of full age, without limitation due to race, nationality or religion, to marry and to found a family, provided marriage is entered into only with the free and full consent of the intending spouses.

The family is described in Article 16 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as the natural and fundamental group unit of society, entitled to protection by society and the State. The term also appears in relation to privacy and to a standard of living adequate for oneself and one’s family.

The State is mentioned in Article 16 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as the political authority that, together with society, must protect the family as the natural and fundamental group unit of society. The term also appears in Article 22 in connection with the organization and resources of each State.

entities.entity_name: Freedom of thought, conscience and religion
entities.description: Freedom of thought, conscience and religion is the set of rights recognized in Article 18 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, including freedom to change one’s religion or belief and to manifest religion or belief in teaching, practice, worship and observance, alone or with others, in public or private.

Freedom of opinion and expression is guaranteed in Article 19 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, including the right to hold opinions without interference and to seek, receive and impart information and ideas through any media and regardless of frontiers.

entities.entity_name: Freedom of peaceful assembly and association
entities.description: Freedom of peaceful assembly and association, as set out in Article 20 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, includes the right to freedom of peaceful assembly and association and the protection against being compelled to belong to an association.

Government is referenced in Article 21 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as the institution whose authority is based on the will of the people, expressed in periodic and genuine elections with universal and equal suffrage and secret or equivalent free voting procedures. Everyone has the right to take part in their government directly or through freely chosen representatives and to equal access to public service.

Periodic and genuine elections are identified in Article 21 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as the mechanism by which the will of the people is expressed, requiring universal and equal suffrage and secret or equivalent free voting procedures.

Universal and equal suffrage is a principle stated in Article 21 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, requiring that elections be by universal and equal suffrage so that everyone has an equal right to vote in periodic and genuine elections.

Social security is identified in Article 22 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as a right of everyone as a member of society, linked to the realization of economic, social and cultural rights indispensable for dignity and the free development of personality, through national effort and international cooperation in accordance with each State’s organization and resources.

Economic, social and cultural rights are described in Article 22 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as rights indispensable for human dignity and the free development of personality, to be realized through national effort and international cooperation according to the organization and resources of each State.

Trade unions are organizations formed by workers to protect their interests. Article 23 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights states that everyone has the right to form and join trade unions for the protection of their interests.
Rest and leisure, including reasonable limitation of working hours and periodic holidays with pay, are recognized in Article 24 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as rights of everyone.

entities.entity_name: Standard of living adequate for health and well-being
entities.description: A standard of living adequate for health and well-being is identified in Article 25 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as a right of everyone, including adequate food, clothing, housing and medical care and necessary social services, and security in cases of unemployment, sickness, disability, widowhood, old age or other lack of livelihood beyond one’s control.
Motherhood is mentioned in Article 25 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as entitled to special care and assistance, along with childhood, in relation to social protection for children.

Childhood is referenced in Article 25 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as entitled to special care and assistance. The article further states that all children, whether born in or out of wedlock, shall enjoy the same social protection.

Education is treated in Article 26 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as a right of everyone, to be free at least in the elementary and fundamental stages, with compulsory elementary education, generally available technical and professional education and equally accessible higher education based on merit. Education is to be directed to the full development of the human personality, the strengthening of respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms, the promotion of understanding, tolerance and friendship among all nations and racial or religious groups, and the furthering of United Nations activities for the maintenance of peace.

The human personality is referenced in Articles 22 and 26 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as something whose free and full development is a goal of economic, social and cultural rights and of education.
The arts are mentioned in Article 27 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as part of the cultural life of the community that everyone has the right to enjoy.
Scientific advancement is mentioned in Article 27 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as something everyone has the right to share in, along with its benefits.

Scientific, literary or artistic production refers to works created by individuals in science, literature or the arts. Article 27 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights states that everyone has the right to the protection of the moral and material interests resulting from any such production of which they are the author.

Social and international order is described in Article 28 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as the overall arrangement of society and international relations in which the rights and freedoms set forth in the Declaration can be fully realized, to which everyone is entitled.

The community is referred to in Articles 22, 27 and 29 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as the social group or society in which individuals live, in which free and full development of personality is possible, and whose cultural life people have the right to participate in. Individuals also have duties to this community.

Morality is mentioned in Article 29 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as one of the just requirements that can justify legal limitations on the exercise of rights and freedoms, alongside public order and the general welfare in a democratic society.

Public order is cited in Article 29 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as one of the purposes that may justify limitations on rights and freedoms, provided such limitations are determined by law to secure recognition and respect for others' rights and freedoms and to meet the just requirements of morality and the general welfare in a democratic society.

entities.entity_name: General welfare in a democratic society
entities.description: The general welfare in a democratic society is mentioned in Article 29 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as one of the just requirements that may justify lawful limitations on rights and freedoms, emphasizing the common good within democratic governance.

entities.entity_name: Purposes and principles of the United Nations
entities.description: The purposes and principles of the United Nations are referenced in Articles 14 and 29 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as standards against which actions are measured. The right to asylum cannot be invoked for acts contrary to these purposes and principles, and rights and freedoms may in no case be exercised contrary to them.

Race is listed in Article 2 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as a prohibited ground of distinction in the enjoyment of the rights and freedoms set forth in the Declaration, and in Article 16 as a characteristic that cannot limit the right of men and women of full age to marry and to found a family.

Language is listed in Article 2 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as a prohibited basis for distinction in the enjoyment of rights and freedoms.

Religion is cited in Article 2 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as a prohibited ground of distinction in the enjoyment of rights and freedoms, mentioned in Article 16 as a characteristic that cannot limit the right to marry and to found a family, and is the subject of the freedom of thought, conscience and religion in Article 18.

Political or other opinion is included in Article 2 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as a prohibited basis for distinction in the enjoyment of rights and freedoms. Relatedly, political status is mentioned in connection with the status of countries or territories.
National or social origin is listed in Article 2 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as a prohibited basis for distinction in the enjoyment of rights and freedoms.

Property is mentioned in Article 2 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as a prohibited ground of distinction in the enjoyment of rights and freedoms, and in Article 17 as something everyone has the right to own and not be arbitrarily deprived of.

Birth is listed in Article 2 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as a prohibited basis for distinction in the enjoyment of rights and freedoms and is implicitly referenced in Article 25, which states that all children, whether born in or out of wedlock, shall enjoy the same social protection.

Other status is a catch-all term in Article 2 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights indicating that distinctions in rights enjoyment are prohibited on any status beyond those explicitly listed, such as race, colour, sex, language and so on.

entities.entity_name: Political, jurisdictional or international status of the country or territory
entities.description: The political, jurisdictional or international status of the country or territory is a composite concept in Article 2 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights stating that no distinction shall be made in the enjoyment of rights and freedoms based on such status, whether the country or territory is independent, trust, non-self-governing or under any other limitation of sovereignty.

Independent status is one of the possible statuses of a country or territory mentioned in Article 2 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, alongside trust and non-self-governing status and other limitations of sovereignty, and is identified as a status that cannot justify distinctions in the enjoyment of rights and freedoms.

Trust territory status is referenced in Article 2 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights by the term "trust", indicating a territory administered under trusteeship. Such status cannot be the basis for distinctions in the enjoyment of rights and freedoms.

Non-self-governing status describes a territory that has not attained full self-government. Article 2 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights states that such a status cannot be a basis for distinctions in the enjoyment of rights and freedoms.

Limitation of sovereignty is referenced in Article 2 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as any other form of restricted sovereignty a country or territory might have, which cannot justify distinctions in the enjoyment of rights and freedoms.

Men and women are referenced in the preamble and Article 16 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as having equal rights, including equal rights to marry and to found a family and equal rights as to marriage, during marriage and at its dissolution.

The human person is referred to in the preamble of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as possessing dignity and worth, and as the subject of fundamental human rights and equal rights of men and women reaffirmed in the Charter of the United Nations.

Children are referenced in Article 25 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as entitled to social protection, with the statement that all children, whether born in or out of wedlock, shall enjoy the same social protection, and that childhood is entitled to special care and assistance.
Barbarous acts are described in the preamble as acts resulting from disregard and contempt for human rights that have outraged the conscience of mankind.
The conscience of mankind is referenced in the preamble as what has been outraged by barbarous acts resulting from disregard and contempt for human rights.
Friendly relations between nations are mentioned in the preamble as something it is essential to promote.
Social progress is mentioned in the preamble as an objective the peoples of the United Nations have determined to promote, alongside better standards of life in larger freedom.

entities.entity_name: Better standards of life in larger freedom
entities.description: Better standards of life in larger freedom are mentioned in the preamble as a goal the peoples of the United Nations have determined to promote.

entities.entity_name: Universal respect for and observance of human rights and fundamental freedoms
entities.description: Universal respect for and observance of human rights and fundamental freedoms is described in the preamble as the objective Member States have pledged themselves, in cooperation with the United Nations, to achieve.

entities.entity_name: Common understanding of rights and freedoms
entities.description: A common understanding of rights and freedoms is described in the preamble as being of the greatest importance for the full realization of the pledge to promote universal respect for and observance of human rights and fundamental freedoms.

entities.entity_name: Every individual and every organ of society
entities.description: Every individual and every organ of society is a phrase in the proclamation stating that all persons and societal bodies shall strive by teaching and education to promote respect for the rights and freedoms in the Declaration and to secure their universal and effective recognition and observance.

Teaching and education are mentioned in the proclamation as means by which every individual and organ of society shall strive to promote respect for the rights and freedoms set forth in the Declaration.

Progressive measures, national and international, are mentioned in the proclamation as actions to secure the universal and effective recognition and observance of the rights and freedoms set forth in the Declaration.

Competent national tribunals are mentioned in Article 8 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as the bodies that provide effective remedies for acts violating fundamental rights granted by the constitution or by law.

An independent and impartial tribunal is mentioned in Article 10 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as the body that must provide a fair and public hearing in determining rights and obligations and any criminal charge.

Constitution or law is mentioned in Article 8 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as the source granting fundamental rights for which individuals may seek an effective remedy by competent national tribunals.

National or international law is mentioned in Article 11 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as the legal systems under which an act or omission must constitute a penal offence at the time it was committed in order for a person to be held guilty.

Honour and reputation are mentioned in Article 12 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as interests protected against attacks, alongside protection against arbitrary interference with privacy, family, home or correspondence.

entities.entity_name: Residence within the borders of each state
entities.description: Residence within the borders of each state is part of the right described in Article 13 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, which states that everyone has the right to freedom of movement and residence within those borders.

Non-political crimes are mentioned in Article 14 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as a category of prosecutions for which the right to seek and enjoy asylum may not be invoked when prosecutions genuinely arise from such crimes.

entities.entity_name: Acts contrary to the purposes and principles of the United Nations
entities.description: Acts contrary to the purposes and principles of the United Nations are mentioned in Article 14 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as another category of acts for which the right to asylum may not be invoked.
Racial or religious groups are mentioned in Article 26 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as groups among whom education shall promote understanding, tolerance and friendship.
Cultural life of the community is mentioned in Article 27 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as a sphere in which everyone has the right freely to participate.

Moral and material interests are mentioned in Article 27 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as interests resulting from scientific, literary or artistic production of which a person is the author and which are to be protected.

Duties to the community are mentioned in Article 29 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as obligations everyone has to the community in which the free and full development of their personality is possible.

A democratic society is referenced in Article 29 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as the context in which the just requirements of morality, public order and the general welfare may justify limitations on rights and freedoms.

Any State, group or person is the phrase used in Article 30 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights to indicate that no entity has any right to engage in activities aimed at destroying the rights and freedoms set forth in the Declaration.

The will of the people is mentioned in Article 21 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as the basis of the authority of government, expressed in periodic and genuine elections with universal and equal suffrage and secret or equivalent free voting procedures.
Public service is mentioned in Article 21 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as a sphere to which everyone has the right of equal access in their country.

Work is mentioned in Article 23 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as a right of everyone, including the right to free choice of employment, just and favourable conditions of work and protection against unemployment.

entities.entity_name: Unemployment, sickness, disability, widowhood and old age
entities.description: Unemployment, sickness, disability, widowhood and old age are listed in Article 25 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as circumstances in which everyone has the right to security as part of an adequate standard of living.

Universal Declaration of Human Rights
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) is a milestone document in the history of human rights. Drafted by representatives with different legal and cultural backgrounds from all regions of the world, the Declaration was proclaimed by the United Nations General Assembly in Paris on 10 December 1948 (General Assembly resolution 217 A) as a common standard of achievements for all peoples and all nations. It sets out, for the first time, fundamental human rights to be universally protected and it has been translated into over 500 languages. The UDHR is widely recognized as having inspired, and paved the way for, the adoption of more than seventy human rights treaties, applied today on a permanent basis at global and regional levels (all containing references to it in their preambles). 

Article 2
Everyone is entitled to all the rights and freedoms set forth in this Declaration, without distinction of any kind, such as race, colour, sex, language, religion, political or other opinion, national or social origin, property, birth or other status. Furthermore, no distinction shall be made on the basis of the political, jurisdictional or international status of the country or territory to which a person belongs, whether it be independent, trust, non-self-governing or under any other limitation of sovereignty.

Article 3
Everyone has the right to life, liberty and security of person.

Article 4
No one shall be held in slavery or servitude; slavery and the slave trade shall be prohibited in all their forms.

Article 5
No one shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.

entities.description: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights is a milestone document in the history of human rights, drafted by representatives from different legal and cultural backgrounds from all regions of the world and proclaimed by the United Nations General Assembly in Paris on 10 December 1948 as General Assembly resolution 217 A, setting out fundamental human rights to be universally protected and serving as a common standard of achievement for all peoples and nations.

UDHR is the acronym for the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, the milestone human rights document proclaimed by the United Nations General Assembly in Paris on 10 December 1948 as General Assembly resolution 217 A and recognized as inspiring more than seventy subsequent human rights treaties.

Human rights are the fundamental rights and freedoms that the Universal Declaration of Human Rights sets out to be universally protected, forming the central subject of the Declaration and of the more than seventy human rights treaties it inspired.

The United Nations General Assembly is the main deliberative body of the United Nations that proclaimed the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in Paris on 10 December 1948 as General Assembly resolution 217 A, describing it as a common standard of achievement for all peoples and all nations.
Paris is the city where the United Nations General Assembly proclaimed the Universal Declaration of Human Rights on 10 December 1948 as General Assembly resolution 217 A.
10 December 1948 is the date on which the United Nations General Assembly, meeting in Paris, proclaimed the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as General Assembly resolution 217 A.
General Assembly resolution 217 A is the formal resolution of the United Nations General Assembly by which the Universal Declaration of Human Rights was proclaimed in Paris on 10 December 1948.

entities.entity_name: More than seventy human rights treaties
entities.description: More than seventy human rights treaties refers to a large number of human rights agreements that were inspired by and followed the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, are applied on a permanent basis at global and regional levels, and contain references to the Declaration in their preambles.

Race is one of the personal characteristics listed in Article 2 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, on which no distinction may be made in enjoying the rights and freedoms set forth in the Declaration.
Colour is one of the grounds listed in Article 2 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights on which discrimination is prohibited in relation to the rights and freedoms in the Declaration.
Sex is one of the characteristics mentioned in Article 2 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights on which no distinction is allowed when granting rights and freedoms under the Declaration.

Language is both a characteristic protected against discrimination under Article 2 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the medium into which the Declaration has been translated over 500 times.
Religion is a protected ground in Article 2 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights; no distinction in the enjoyment of rights and freedoms may be made based on a person’s religion.

Political or other opinion is a category of belief listed in Article 2 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights on which discrimination is prohibited in relation to the rights and freedoms set forth in the Declaration.

National or social origin is a personal attribute mentioned in Article 2 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights that cannot be used as a basis for distinction in the enjoyment of the Declaration’s rights and freedoms.

Property is one of the statuses listed in Article 2 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, indicating that distinctions in rights and freedoms cannot be based on whether or what property a person owns.

Текст Декларации явился результатом тесного взаимодействия специалистов в области права, представлявших все регионы планеты. Впервые в истории человечества был принят документ, провозгласивший необходимость защиты основных прав человека. Декларация переведена на 500 языков.

Статья 2
Каждый человек должен обладать всеми правами и всеми свободами, провозглашенными настоящей Декларацией, без какого бы то ни было различия, как-то в отношении расы, цвета кожи, пола, языка, религии, политических или иных убеждений, национального или социального происхождения, имущественного, сословного или иного положения.

Кроме того, не должно проводиться никакого различия на основе политического, правового или международного статуса страны или территории, к которой человек принадлежит, независимо от того, является ли эта территория независимой, подопечной, несамоуправляющейся или как-либо иначе ограниченной в своем суверенитете.

Статья 3
Каждый человек имеет право на жизнь, на свободу и на личную неприкосновенность.

Статья 4
Никто не должен содержаться в рабстве или в подневольном состоянии; рабство и работорговля запрещаются во всех их видах.

Статья 5
Никто не должен подвергаться пыткам или жестоким, бесчеловечным или унижающим его достоинство обращению и наказанию.

19 A ‘Mineral Resource’ is a concentration or occurrence of material of
economic interest in or on the Earth’s crust in such form, quality and quantity
that there are reasonable prospects for eventual economic extraction. The
location, quantity, grade, continuity and other geological characteristics of a
Mineral Resource are known, estimated or interpreted from specific geological
evidence, sampling and knowledge. Mineral Resources are subdivided, in
order of increasing geological confidence into Inferred, Indicated and
Measured categories.

Portions of a mineral deposit that do not have reasonable prospects for eventual
economic extraction must not be included in a Mineral Resource.

The term ‘Mineral Resource’ covers mineralisation, including dumps and tailings,
which has been identified and estimated through exploration and sampling and within
which Mineral Reserves may be defined by the consideration and application of
Modifying Factors.

The term ‘reasonable prospects for eventual economic extraction’ implies a
judgement (albeit preliminary) by the Competent Person in respect of the technical
and economic factors likely to influence the prospect of economic extraction,
including the approximate mining parameters. In other words, a Mineral Resource is
not an inventory of all mineralisation drilled or sampled, regardless of cut-off grade,
likely mining dimensions, location or continuity. It is a realistic inventory of
mineralisation which, under assumed and justifiable technical and economic
conditions, might, in whole or in part, become economically extractable.

entities.description: A defined term for a concentration or occurrence of material of economic interest in or on the Earth’s crust, in such form, quality, and quantity that there are reasonable prospects for eventual economic extraction. Its location, quantity, grade, continuity, and other geological characteristics are known, estimated, or interpreted from specific geological evidence, sampling, and knowledge. Mineral Resources are subdivided into Inferred, Indicated, and Measured categories in order of increasing geological confidence and cover mineralisation, including dumps and tailings, within which Mineral Reserves may be defined by applying Modifying Factors. A Mineral Resource is described as a realistic inventory of mineralisation that might, in whole or in part, become economically extractable under assumed and justifiable technical and economic conditions, and explicitly is not an inventory of all mineralisation drilled or sampled regardless of economic prospects.

Material of economic interest occurring in or on the Earth’s crust that forms the subject of a Mineral Resource definition and must be in such form, quality, and quantity that there are reasonable prospects for eventual economic extraction.

The outermost solid shell of the Earth where material of economic interest may occur in or on it; Mineral Resources are defined as concentrations or occurrences of such material in or on the Earth’s crust.

Specific geological data and information that provide the basis for knowing, estimating, or interpreting the location, quantity, grade, continuity, and other geological characteristics of a Mineral Resource.

The process of taking samples of geological material used, together with geological evidence and knowledge, to estimate or interpret the characteristics of a Mineral Resource and to identify and estimate mineralisation, including dumps and tailings.

The Inferred category of Mineral Resources, representing the lowest level of geological confidence in the subdivision of Mineral Resources into categories of increasing geological confidence (Inferred, Indicated, and Measured).

The Indicated category of Mineral Resources, representing an intermediate level of geological confidence, higher than Inferred and lower than Measured, in the subdivision of Mineral Resources by geological confidence.
The Measured category of Mineral Resources, representing the highest level of geological confidence in the subdivision of Mineral Resources into Inferred, Indicated, and Measured categories.

A naturally occurring accumulation of minerals in the Earth’s crust; the text notes that portions of a mineral deposit that do not have reasonable prospects for eventual economic extraction must not be included in a Mineral Resource.

entities.entity_name: Portions of a mineral deposit without reasonable prospects for eventual economic extraction
entities.description: Those portions of a mineral deposit that do not have reasonable prospects for eventual economic extraction and therefore must not be included in a Mineral Resource.

Mineralised material that has been identified and estimated through exploration and sampling and is covered by the term ‘Mineral Resource’, including material such as dumps and tailings, within which Mineral Reserves may later be defined.

Accumulations of mined material, typically waste or low-grade material stored on surface, that are explicitly included under the term ‘Mineral Resource’ when they have been identified and estimated through exploration and sampling.

Residues left over from processing ore, typically stored in tailings facilities, that are explicitly included under the term ‘Mineral Resource’ when they have been identified and estimated through exploration and sampling.

The economically mineable part of a Mineral Resource, referenced as being definable within a Mineral Resource by the consideration and application of Modifying Factors, although not otherwise detailed in the text.

A collective term for the technical, economic, and other relevant factors that are considered and applied to a Mineral Resource in order to define Mineral Reserves; their consideration determines whether parts of a Mineral Resource can be classified as Mineral Reserves.

entities.entity_name: Reasonable prospects for eventual economic extraction
entities.description: A requirement that a Mineral Resource must have reasonable prospects for eventual economic extraction. It implies a judgement, albeit preliminary, by the Competent Person in respect of the technical and economic factors likely to influence the prospect of economic extraction, including approximate mining parameters, and distinguishes a Mineral Resource from a mere inventory of all mineralisation drilled or sampled.

A qualified individual responsible for making a preliminary judgement on the technical and economic factors likely to influence the prospect of economic extraction when assessing whether there are reasonable prospects for eventual economic extraction of a Mineral Resource.

Approximate mining-related parameters, including engineering and operational aspects, that form part of the technical factors considered by the Competent Person when judging reasonable prospects for eventual economic extraction of a Mineral Resource.

The cut-off grade referenced as one of the criteria that distinguish a Mineral Resource from an inventory of all mineralisation drilled or sampled; the text notes that a Mineral Resource is not an inventory regardless of cut-off grade, implying that cut-off grade is a factor in defining a realistic inventory of mineralisation.

The likely size and shape of the mining operation, cited as one of the factors in the statement that a Mineral Resource is not simply an inventory of all mineralisation drilled or sampled regardless of likely mining dimensions.

The spatial location and continuity of mineralisation, identified as one of the geological characteristics used to define a Mineral Resource and as one of the factors that differentiates a Mineral Resource from a simple inventory of all mineralisation drilled or sampled.

An inventory of mineralisation described as realistic under assumed and justifiable technical and economic conditions, representing material that might, in whole or in part, become economically extractable, and contrasted with an inventory of all mineralisation drilled or sampled.
